subtopic: MIDDLE EAST-REQUEST FOR STATEMENT OF CANADIAN POSITION

speechtext: On the orders of the day:

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader
subtopic: MIDDLE EAST-REQUEST FOR STATEMENT OF CANADIAN POSITION
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I wish to direct a question to the right hon. Prime Minister and ask him if, as a result of his talks with the Prime Minister of Great Britain, Mr. Wilson, he can inform parliament whether Canada has given any undertakings as to a joint statement regarding the gulf of Aqaba. I ask this question because I am sure the Prime Minister is aware that such a suggestion was made in the House of Lords the other day by Lord Avon, who was prime minister at the time of the Suez crisis in 1956. I wish to ask whether Canada is to participate in a declaration to the effect that the gulf of Aqaba is an international waterway.

speakeroldname: Right Hon. L. B. Pearson (Prime Minister):
subtopic: MIDDLE EAST-REQUEST FOR STATEMENT OF CANADIAN POSITION
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, the question of participation in a collective declaration regarding action of this kind has not come up. There has been no discussion of participation with other governments in any declaration of this nature. On the question of a declaration by this and other governments expressing the views they have taken in the past-I am now thinking of Canada-as to the right of freedom of passage, innocent passage, through the strait of Tiran into the gulf of Aqaba, we have already made a declaration as a government that we take this view, and if it is necessary to repeat that declaration we will do so and are willing to do so. That is quite apart from any general collective declaration as to what might or might not be done in this particular situation.

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader
subtopic: MIDDLE EAST-REQUEST FOR STATEMENT OF CANADIAN POSITION
speechtext: A supplementary question, Mr. Speaker. I ask the right hon. Prime Minister whether during the discussions with the British Prime Minister or any other discussions the government might have had with U Thant at the United Nations the government has committed or is committing Canada to any definite course. If so I wish to ask the Prime Minister, if there are any commitments or if there will be commitments, will he undertake to consult parliament prior to entering into commitments on behalf of Canada?

subtopic: MIDDLE EAST-REQUEST FOR STATEMENT OF CANADIAN POSITION
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the only commitments we have in this matter are the commitments we have undertaken under the charter of the United Nations. No other commitments have been given; no other commitments have been asked. This general matter is being considered now at the United Nations

in the security council. No doubt there will be resolutions submitted to the security council dealing with the matter my hon. friend has raised, and we shall take our position at the security council as a member of the United Nations in respect of these particular resolutions if and when they are produced; but we have no commitment to anyone beyond the commitments we have undertaken in this country and in this parliament arising out of our membership in the United Nations.

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader
subtopic: MIDDLE EAST-REQUEST FOR STATEMENT OF CANADIAN POSITION
speechtext: I would ask the Prime Minister this question. Will he undertake to advise parliament or seek parliament's advice before making any commitments beyond the commitments that we have with the United Nations?

subtopic: MIDDLE EAST-REQUEST FOR STATEMENT OF CANADIAN POSITION
speechtext: I answered that question yesterday, I think, Mr. Speaker. I said if there was any question of this country undertaking any commitments that involved the use of force in any way, parliament would be consulted.

subtopic: MIDDLE EAST-REQUEST FOR STATEMENT OF CANADIAN POSITION
speechtext: May I follow up the same problem, Mr. Speaker. I ask the right hon. gentleman whether an earlier answer of his means that in the view of the government of Canada there is no purpose in a declaration by the maritime powers at this time such as I understand Mr. Wilson to have proposed, because that would be merely reiterating a previous declaration.

subtopic: MIDDLE EAST-REQUEST FOR STATEMENT OF CANADIAN POSITION
speechtext: Consideration has been given to this point by the government of the United States and the government of the United Kingdom, and Mr. Wilson indicated to us yesterday the kind of declaration he thought might be desirable in certain circumstances-and by "circumstances" I mean if the security council were completely frustrated and unable to take any action at all. But that point has not yet been reached.

subtopic: MIDDLE EAST-REQUEST FOR STATEMENT OF CANADIAN POSITION
speechtext:
I should like to ask the Prime
Minister whether the latest developments in the security council hold out any hope that some effective result may be obtained.

subtopic: MIDDLE EAST-REQUEST FOR STATEMENT OF CANADIAN POSITION
speechtext:
Well, I am always optimistic, Mr. Speaker, but I quite agree with what the hon. member has implied in his question; they are having great difficulty in the security council at the present time in agreeing on a resolution which would be acceptable to everybody.
June 2. 1967

subtopic: MIDDLE EAST-REQUEST FOR STATEMENT OF CANADIAN POSITION
speechtext: We know the attitude of the Canadian government toward this waterway, but does the government intend to sponsor or seek a collective declaration by the security council respecting the gulf of Aqaba?

subtopic: MIDDLE EAST-REQUEST FOR STATEMENT OF CANADIAN POSITION
speechtext: This is exactly the matter which is now before the security council, or at least which is being discussed at the United Nations by consultations among individual members of that council.

subtopic: MIDDLE EAST-REQUEST FOR STATEMENT OF CANADIAN POSITION
speechtext: Although I constitute only 1.05 per cent of the second largest party in the house, might I presume a broader representation and ask the Prime Minister whether he would convey to the C.B.C. appreciation for airing the press conference of the British Prime Minister this morning, and to that distinguished gentleman for his lucid, thoughtful and helpful contribution to our understanding of world affairs.

subtopic: MIDDLE EAST-REQUEST FOR STATEMENT OF CANADIAN POSITION
speechtext: Hear, hear.

subtopic: MIDDLE EAST-REQUEST FOR STATEMENT OF CANADIAN POSITION
speechtext: should like to ask the Prime Minister another supplementary question. In his discussions with the Prime Minister of Great Britain was any consideration given to the unfortunate situation of some 750 Arab displaced persons? This appears to be a festering point, one which has caused a lot of this difficulty. Was there any discussion of this matter with a view to finding permanent settlement for these people?

subtopic: MIDDLE EAST-REQUEST FOR STATEMENT OF CANADIAN POSITION
speechtext: This is a question which has been under discussion at the United Nations and outside it for several years. It is not a question of 750 displaced persons but of 750,000 displaced persons. I agree with the hon. member that this is one of the complicating and tragic elements of the whole situation and one which over the years has been causing trouble.

Mr. Speaker, I am very grateful to have the opportunity to tell hon. members of the house what the prospects are for the summer adjournment. Mr. Chairman, before reporting on the situation in the Post Office Department, I should like to acquaint the house with my personal views and feelings about that department after a year and a half of a very close relationship.
Of course, we all deal constantly with the Post Office Department, because that government agency is, in a way, part of our daily life and succeeds in providing us with numerous services without ever betraying our secrets.
During my trips across Canada, I had the opportunity to meet postmen, mail clerks, rural postmasters, rural mail couriers and postal agents, all people whose devotion to duty ensures the proper operation of the Canadian postal service.
Need I say, Mr. Chairman, that these people are not simply a group of employees working for any business, they are the employees of the Canadian post office, that is to say the very people who give Canada the best mail service in the world and who show that they are determined not to let the Canadian postal service become involved in operating difficulties as experienced by other postal services.
Too often, when an organization does a job quietly and efficiently from year to year, those who benefit from this quiet efficiency come to look upon it as the most natural thing in the world. Who ever thinks of the complications of post office operations and of the vast planning job always necessary to maintain a good service in a rapidly developing country?
After a year and a half, I have come to know this lively department, of which I am proud to be a part. I am proud to present today for the third time, the estimates of the
Supply-Post Office
Post Office Department, the moneys we require for the operating costs of the department during 1967-68.
A glance at the figures for the fiscal year 1965-66 on which was based our last report will give everyone an idea of the wide operations of the Post Office Department and of the enlightened management which is needed, as shown by the report of expenditures and revenues.
About 4,600 million mail items are now handled every year. That comes to 240 items per year per man, woman and child in Canada. This figure can be considered as a rate of increase, since every time the population of Canada increases by one person, the post office must be ready to handle 240 items more a year.
Mail carriers, urban and rural, are now serving 4,100,000 business and private calls. The handing of mail and service to the public give occupation to 44,244 employees in 11,172 post offices. The revenues in cash amounted to $276 million, while the expenditures amounted to $279 million. One must take into account other revenue amounting to $9 million for postal services to other departments and parliament against expenditures set at $36.5 million for local services to the Post Office Department by the other federal agencies. If those estimates are added to the cash revenue and to the expenditures, the Post Office Department shows an operating deficit of $30.5 million, since the total revenue amounted to $285 million, whereas the expenditures totalled $315.1 million.
[DOT] (11:50 a.m.)
The increased rates announced for some services, such as parcel post, third class mail, registered mail, special delivery and C.O.D. shipments, which will become effective on June 1 and October 1 of this year, will help to reduce the deficit of the Post Office Department, but the trend towards an increase in costs, for transportation as well as labour, might maintain expenditures at a higher level than the revenue. This fact becomes even more obvious when one realizes that transportation and labour account for approximately 89 per cent of the post office total expenditures.
However, one must not consider only the financial aspect of the operation of the Post Office Department. The Canadian post office is something more than a mere mail processing plant. It is not only a matter of receipts and expenditures. It also concerns the people.

June 2, 1967
Supply-Post Office
It is a matter of buildings, and working conditions. It is also a matter of a service rendered to the entire population and to the country.
If it had been otherwise, it would not have been necessary to create a royal commission on working conditions in the Post Office Department. The report of the royal commission, tabled on October 19, 1966, contained 282 recommendations dealing with a great number of subjects related to labour relations as a whole within the postal organization.
On behalf of the department, Mr. Chairman, I say that we heartily welcomed the report. All of us must congratulate the commissioner, Justice Andre Montpetit, and his advisers for their speed and perseverance during the inquiry and for the depth of perception evidenced in their study of the problems of the Post Office Department.
The report points out that the Canadian people are well served and that the credit goes to the department and its employees. It insists that none of the recommendations is intended to reduce the quality of the service given the public. It indicates, however, and very deary, the need for a certain number of radical reforms in working conditions and in employer-employee relations. Those reforms, as mentioned in the report, will result from the implementation of collective bargaining and from the grievance procedure provided by the legislation on collective bargaining.
All through the report, the need for systematic discussions between management and representatives of the employees is emphasized in order to discover problems of mutual interest, to explain to the employees the nature of any major change affecting their working conditions and to obtain their views with regard to any change before its implementation.
That is the spirit and the method which the Post Office Department has decided to use in order to implement the recommendations contained in the report and which are fully within its control.
A commission made up of department officers and representatives of the Postal Workers Union of Canada and the Mail Carriers Union of Canada holds regular meetings for a joint consideration of a selected number of recommendations. That commission operates in such a friendly atmosphere that the postal service and the news media receive joint statements as to progress made.
[Mr. Cote (Longueuil) .1

To date 57 recommendations have been adopted and another 67 are reaching the stage of agreement or at least acceptable understanding. Yet another 60 are receiving preliminary study. Along with this action a grievance procedure has been developed and issued for implementation. Labour-management committees will be established in all the staff post offices. Consultation with the unions as to the composition and terms of reference of these committees is now under way.
The Post Office Department has had under study the feasibility and economics of operating its own trucks in the larger Canadian cities for the delivery of parcel post, letter carrier bundles and special delivery, and for the clearance of street letter boxes. Last December a labour-management dispute between the Montreal contractor for the city services and his employees temporarily threatened the postal service in that city and elsewhere, as Montreal is a key point in the over-all Canadian mail system. This was a case of the Canada post office being a third party in an industrial dispute. The short work stoppage which resulted in curtailed mail service emphasized the need to accelerate the study of post office operated vehicles.
The department has owned and operated vehicles in the city of Windsor, Ontario, with a marked degree of success. Whether it is more economical to own and operate or lease and operate is the question to be decided. All calculations would indicate the latter to be the better arrangement. To prove this, areas in Montreal and Vancouver have been selected for pilot project study. Arrangements to lease vehicles have been made. They will go into operation July 1 in the area selected at both centres.
The dislocation this move will cause to employees of the contractors in Vancouver and Montreal has been taken into consideration. The employees of the contractors will have every right to apply for positions in the government operated service. As they are experienced in the duties to be performed, such as an intimate knowledge of the area to be served, the method of delivery and the mail pick-up system, they will naturally receive a high knowledge rating if and when they apply for employment with the Post Office Department.
If tests bear out the favourable forecast made for this type of operation, the Post Office Department will move forward to total operation of its transportation services in the larger centres where leased fleet operations
June 2, 1967

can be more efficient and economical than the old contractual arrangements.
Mr. Chairman, I trust my remarks will give the members some idea of the action behind the scenes that keeps the letter carrier on the street, that keeps the rural mail driver on the road, that keeps the postal clerk behind the wicket and that keeps each and every one of them at their appointed task of providing a top flight mail service to the people of Canada. It was interesting to listen to the C.B.C. radio program "Court of Opinions" at 8.30 p.m. May 26, when the panel discussed the question "Do we have a well operated postal service?" Probably the members will not believe it when I say this question was not planted, but I can say I was happy with the unanimous opinion of the panel, and I am sure the members will understand my elation, because the consensus was that Canada does indeed have a well operated postal service.
Mr. Chairman, having quoted that favourable opinion I will close my remarks and ask hon. members of the house to earnestly consider the amounts represented by the estimates which I consider are necessary to continue to provide our country with a well operated postal service.
[DOT] (12 noon)

Mr. Chairman, my first remarks must be to compliment and thank the minister for his statement. Many questions I had in mind were answered in the statement which has just been concluded.
If I might be permitted a personal reference to the gentleman who holds the distinguished portfolio of Postmaster General, I should like to say that in my opinion he has brought a very pleasant personality to the office, which has been reflected in a reasonable and courteous attitude toward the many requests made of him by members of this chamber. Personally I have had many dealings with the department through him, the last of which was no later than today. However, nothing has impressed me more than his personal attention to a matter dealing with obscene and hate literature passing through the mails which was recently brought to my attention. This information was relayed to the minister who immediately took action, and within hours the mailing privileges of this despicable organization were cancelled.
I compliment the minister on his attitude, and I wish him well. I would remind hon. members that he is the seventh postmaster general we have had since 1962. We seem to change postmaster generals as often as we 27053-69
Supply-Post Office
change the styles of ladies' hats. However, Mr. Chairman, if we have to put up with this government then our present Postmaster General will, I hope, continue in office, even though he has already lasted longer than the average over the last five years.
I should like to refer to the summation of the minister on May 19 last, which is to be found at page 5331 of Hansard. The Postmaster General said as follows:
When my colleague, the present Minister of Labour, was postmaster general, he supported the recommendation of the Glassco commission for the adoption by my department of a more suitable accounting system to identify all the accounts receivable by the department and all its financial charges, in order to get a clearer picture of the department's financial position.
I am positive, Mr. Chairman, that many members in this chamber are as confused as I am about our accounting procedures. I should like to refer for a moment to the abridged report of the public accounts of Canada for the fiscal year 1966. In the statement of expenditure and revenue the amount shown for the Post Office Department by way of expenditure is $240,206,458. The post office revenue is shown as $237,482,296, which gives a deficit of $2,724,162. Yet I am sure I heard the Postmaster General say this morning there was a deficit of $30.5 million.
I concur completely with his statement last year that we should have some simplified accounting procedure, but there is quite a difference in amount here. I presume there is a simple explanation for it, but frankly I am not an auditor. As I say, according to the abridged report of the public accounts a deficit of $2,700,000 is shown. In the estimates for 1966 we find that the cost of franked mail was $1,262,200. If that amount is by-passed, the Post Office Department had an actual deficit of $1,400,000.
In report No. 21 of the proceedings of the standing committee on public accounts for October 13, 1966 a statement appears which admittedly is based on 1965 figures, and I should like to put it on record:
The committee notes that whereas the Post Office Department's transactions recorded in the post office section of volume II of the public accounts for the year ended March 31, 1965 showed an excess of revenue over expenditure of $20,030,000, this financial result did not take into account other expenditures estimated at $35.8 million and other revenues estimated at $4.3 million. If this unrecorded expenditure and revenue had been taken into the accounts, the operating deficit of the Post Office Department for the year ended March 31, 1965 would have been $11.5 million instead of the excess of revenue over expenditure, or surplus, shown at $20,030,000 for the year.

June 2, 1967
Supply-Post Office
Now, Mr. Chairman, what gives here? There seems to me to be quite a difference between these figures and those in the abridged report. I hope there is a good explanation for this, and I expect the minister will answer this question when he replies.
If I may refer back to the committee report, the next paragraph reads as follows:
The committe also notes that if the loss incurred by the Post Office Department from second class mail had been recaptured, it would have more than covered this operating deficit of $11.5 million for the 1965 fiscal year. In 1956-57 postal revenues from second class mail were $6 million, with the Post Office Department estimating the cost of handling it at $24 million. Seven years later, or in 1963-64, these revenues had increased to slightly over $8 million while the cost of handling it was estimated by the Post Office Department to have exceeded $43 million, resulting in a loss of $35 million. The committee regretted that no figures were available on May 25, 1966 showing the size of losses incurred on second class mail in 1964-65 or in 1965-66.
The committee feels that there is something wrong when no action has been taken with respect to, and apparently very little consideration given to, its recommendation on this matter. The committee first drew the matter to the attention of the house in its third report 1958 and, while minor changes have been made, the annual loss has continued to increase and the committee is of the opinion that sufficient consideration has not been given to the solution of this problem.
The next sentence, Mr. Chairman, is a gem:
It considers it essential that the Post Office Department or parliament immediately find ways and means of covering the loss of the Post Office Department in handling second class mail without this being done at the expense of other classes of mail, keeping in mind, however, the need of assistance to small independently owned newspapers circulating in rural areas.
My question to the minister at this juncture is an obvious one. What plans are afoot to correct this situation?
Last year the hon. member for York-Humber raised the question of the international postal agreement and compared second and third class mailings as between Canada and Denmark. I should like to inquire of the minister what is the relative volume of second and third class United States mail handled by our post office that brings in no revenue. In other words, can the minister give me the relative figures? How much second or third class Canadian mail goes to the United States and how much United States mail of that kind comes into Canada? What is our net loss in this transaction? It has been suggested in certain circles that our taxpayers are paying between $1.5 million to $2 million for deliveries, for example, of Time and Reader's Digest. I should like the minister to say

whether that is so. Is what I have said correct? If so, what is to be done?
[DOT] (12:10 p.m.)
I wish to mention something else now, the cost of franked mail in Canada. On page 381 of the blue book of estimates the estimated cost of franked mail for the current year is shown as $1,124,600. The amount shown for last year was $1,262,200. The cost this year has decreased by approximately $147,600. Perhaps the next question is unnecessary but I shall ask it none the less. Was the large) amount in the previous year occasioned by the bad advice the President of the Privy Council gave the Prime Minister about a date in November, 1965?
It could be.

If so, I think the Canadian public is entitled to know that besides the advertised costs they have also to foot the bill for some hidden expenses whenever there is an election. If this is the situation I think it is a dashed shame.
I note something else. In 1966 we paid $381,700 to cover exhibits, advertising, films, broadcasting and displays. What does that mean? What films, broadcasts or advertising does the department put out, other than "Mail early before Christmas"? I know of no other program. Surely we are not advertising that our stamps are better than Steinberg's pinky stamps or gold bond stamps?
It is a coincidence that we should be discussing the estimates of the Post Office Department today when yesterday the department put into effect an unprecedented 45 per cent increase in some postal rates. Where is this escalation in the cost of living to stop? I wish to give an example of the new rates for registered mail. Until yesterday you could register a letter with a value of up to $25 for 35 cents; today that same letter will cost 50 cents. That is an increase of 45 per cent. Yesterday you could register a letter with a value of up $50 for 45 cents; today that letter costs 50 cents to register. Yesterday a letter with a value of up to $75 cost 50 cents to register, and today it costs 75 cents to register. That is an increase of 50 per cent. This is an example of how ordinary people are being forced to pay for the loss leader part of the operation.
In fairness to the minister I must say that he is all heart when it comes to mailing postcards to foreign places. All postcards were charged at letter rates, but now you can
June 2, 1967



send a postcard to Japan, say, for 10 cents, or to any part of the world for that matter. The cost used to be 25 cents for that privilege. I submit that this sort of thing does not help Canadians very much, though I expect our tourists are happy at the reduced rates on postcards.
In conclusion, I hope the minister has some plan in mind to implement the all-embracing recommendation of the public accounts committee. May I repeat a sentence from that committee report to be found on page 1007 of the proceedings of Thursday, October 13, 1966:
It considers it essential that the Post Office Department or parliament immediately find ways and means of covering the loss of the Post Office Department in handling second class mail without this being done at the expense of other classes of mail, keeping in mind however the need of assistance to small independently owned newspapers circulating in rural areas.
If what is outlined there can be done, then I suggest that our present Postmaster General will go down in history as a world's champion.

Mr. Chairman, I am grateful to the Postmaster General for mentioning in his introductory remarks the new policy that his department is to follow on an experimental basis in two of the major cities of Canada. On July 1 the government is to take over from Pony Express Limited the bulk of the collection and delivery of mail, and the parcel post business. I have talked to the minister and corresponded with him about the situation in the city of Vancouver, and I wish to thank him for the expeditious way he has answered my letters and for his readiness to discuss the entire matter with me.
Though I do not object to the principles involved in the takeover I object strongly to how the takeover is to be conducted and how it will affect the employees concerned. I regret that I have to raise this matter on this first vote of the department to be considered. I cannot speak for Montreal, but I know that in my own city of Vancouver the collection and distribution of mail which the minister spoke of has been carried on by Pony Express Limited, that is by private agents. In talking and corresponding with me and in what he said today the minister made it clear that there are two major reasons for this change which is to be made on July 1.
One reason is understandable and stems from the recent experience in Montreal, 27053-691
Supply-Post Office
when the postal service of Canada was disrupted because of a strike against the company holding the postal contract. The strike directly affected the receipt and delivery of all mail in Montreal and the dispatch of letters and parcels throughout Canada and elsewhere. The minister also informed me that it is the conclusion of the department that economies could be effected were the Post Office Department to handle mail in my area. I will not challenge the contentious propositions of the minister as to why the change is to be made. I wish to speak, sir, on behalf of employees in the city of Vancouver, some of whom have occupied their positions for 25 years, and of their position when the government takes over from private enterprise.
[DOT] (12:20 p.ra.)
Surely those in Vancouver who have been doing this job for 25 years know the work. What consideration was given to these employees? It would seem to me that when the government takes over on July 1 the efficient thing to do would be to take on these employees who know the pick-ups and the deliveries. Is that how the government operates? No; they will not be taken into the civil service as employees of the Post Office Department. They are out unless they make application to the civil service commission. Advertisements have been placed in the papers inviting people to apply for employment as truck drivers, but there are only two kinds of driver; those who have been doing this job and know it, and those who have never worked in this kind of employment and do not know one thing about it.
Until ten days ago-and I thank the minister for his letters to me-only three of the Pony Express drivers in Vancouver had made application for these jobs. Why is this number so small in comparison with the number of men who are being displaced? It is because those who have worked for this company in Vancouver for as long as 25 years are being asked to apply for employment in the civil service at lower wages than they have been receiving. How can men who know the work, men with years of loyal service behind them, be asked to apply for positions in the civil service and work for the government for substantially lower wages?
There is another important point, I know, to be considered. If I understand the situation correctly the Public Service Employees Association-speaking from memory I believe there are around 20,000 in this group-want a

June 2, 1967
Supply-Post Office
national standard of wages. I agree in principle with those who wish to see a national standard of wages, but I do not believe that when the government takes over an operation from private enterprise the standard of living of the employees should suffer. In Vancouver the department is lowering the standard, lowering the wages; and I say as emphatically as I can that no government when it takes over an operation of this kind has the right to lower the standards of any worker in Canada or to worsen the working conditions of our people in Vancouver. If the union wants a national wage standard, fine; but let it not be achieved on the basis of lowering standards in the west so as to raise them in the east. Raise them in the east, but do not lower them in the west. Hold the west.
To me it is almost incomprehensible that any department of this government would wish to lower standards, yet the contract basis upon which the post office is working now is designed to raise them in the east while lowering them in the west. No wonder that until ten days ago only three of the truck drivers of the Pony Express company in Vancouver had made application to the civil service in connection with these jobs.
Am I not putting forward a reasonable case, Mr. Chairman? When a move is made from free enterprise to public operation let us not lower the standards of employees, even if ultimately a national wage standard is required in order to simplify the general bargaining picture. Do not reduce the wages and standards of the west. Hold them, if you have to, until the rest of Canada catches up. I think it is a nasty day in the history of Canada when the government, taking over from private enterprise, decides to reduce wages and worsen working conditions. Surely something else could be done.
I appreciate the government's point of view. I hope economies can be made by means of greater efficiency. But, I repeat, to me it seems despicable that a government should take over an operation without arranging that those who have given their loyalty to their previous employers, those who know the job, are not taken over automatically to continue the work which they and they only understand.
[DOT] (12:30 p.m.)
I think it is a denial of so-called liberalism that with regard to standards you should, on a national basis, increase standards in some areas and decrease them in others. I believe the minister should hold to the standards
IMr. Winch.]
which are highest and bring the others up to that level. Heaven forbid that we should have a government policy to reduce standards, but that is what is being done in Vancouver, and that is what will happen after July 1. I hope there is still time between now and then to correct this policy which I think is absolutely immoral and, if I may say so, very unpolitical.

Mr. Chairman, on entering the discussion of the estimates of the Post Office Department I wish to make a few brief and pertinent remarks. I had a survey made in my constituency of all mail courier contracts, and I wish to thank the Postmaster General and his staff for the courtesy they extended me and for the material with which they supplied me.
It is interesting but also disappointing to learn that for similar mileage there should be such a discrepancy in rates paid per contract. True, there are some different aspects which enter into the picture, such as the number of mail boxes on a route, but there are also other factors which must be considered, such as the terrain travelled by the couriers. For instance, carrying out a mail contract on a highway, county or improved road is certainly much easier in wintertime, because such roads are patrol plowed several times a day, than is the case with a contract covering back roads, which quite often are not plowed every day. Further, when the spring breakup comes many back roads are almost impassable, and sometimes a mail courier losses the muffler or oil pan off his car. This is an added expense to him because he must keep his car in safe condition at all times.
Today highways and new improved roads are built with a 7 degree to 9 degree incline and descent, but back roads are not constructed to that standard. They still have steep hills which are subject to washouts in the spring. This involves much braking going down hill and changing of gears going up hill, which cuts down the mileage per gallon which a courier gets with his car. In this connection I would point out that the spring of 1967, which has just ended, was one of the worst so far as roads were concerned.
The survey I spoke of is confidential, but I feel that the discrepancy in rates should be corrected. To give a few examples from the survey, one courier on a route covering 27.9 miles per day, six days a week, receives $2,768.62 per annum. Another on a route of 28.1 miles per day, six days a week, receives $1,985.91 per annum. This is a difference of
June 2, 1967

$782.71 per annum. The first contract of which I speak was renewed in 1965 and the second in 1966, and we all know that the price of gas, automobile insurance and car repairs, not to mention the cost of living, has been spiralling since 1965.
If we take the minimum wage scale of $1.25 per hour, using a 20 mile per day route and an average work day of three hours, this would work out at $3.75 per courier, plus $2 for gas at 10 cents per mile, making a total of $5.75 per day. In a normal year a mail courier would work at least 307 days, and this would give him a minimum contract pay of $1,765.25.
I give three examples from the survey. One route of 20 miles provides the courier with $1,380.10 per annum. A second route of 20.2 miles provides the courier with $1,326.26 per annum. A third of 20 miles provides $1,470,00, and a fourth route of 18.7 miles provides the courier with $2,100.00. There is quite a discrepancy there. I could make many more comparisons, but at this stage am content to recommend that a full review be made, with the hope that it will result in equalization of remuneration for equal work hours and miles driven.
I wish to commend the Postmaster General for putting identification on cars carrying rural mail. When I spoke on his estimates previously I made that recommendation. The minister sent me a note saying he thought it had merit. He has now implemented it, and I want to thank him for that. I would also like to commend the minister for introducing door to door mail delivery in the town of Orangeville. I requested such service as far back as 1963, and now four years later it has been provided.
I would like to make one suggestion to the minister respecting flexibility in interpretation of the act. According to the manual, people in small hamlets must live a certain distance from the post office before they can have their mail delivered to rural mail boxes. Quite often small hamlets are made up of retired elderly people. Because these hamlets do not have sidewalks their inhabitants must walk on the roads. Poor eyesight and bad hearing create hazards both for the pedestrians and for motor traffic, and I believe that in certain cases the minister and the department could consider having mail delivered to rural boxes even though those boxes are within the distance specified by the act.
Like my colleague from Lambton-Kent I would like to express thanks to the Postmaster General for the many courtesies he
Supply-Post Office
has extended to me and for his prompt attention to matters that I brought to his attention.

Mr. Chairman, I have a few comments I would like to make with regard to rates on second class mail. I made them previously, but I am afraid the attention that was paid to them then presages the attention that will be paid to them now.
[DOT] (12:40 p.m.)
I would draw the attention of the committee to the fact that I spoke last year before the public accounts committee of the House of Commons with regard to postage rates on second class mail. At the time I asked a number of questions, and I was advised by officials of the Post Office Department that I would receive the answers I requested. Since I am a patient man I am still patiently waiting for these details. I shall repeat the questions now in the hope that they will be answered before the public accounts committee meets again, because I intend to appear before that committee again if necessary.
One of the questions I raised before the public accounts committee with regard to postal rates had to do with the rate per pound being paid for air mail transmission. At page 385 of the blue book under vote No. 1 you will find the following: Mail service by railway, $14,660,000; mail service by ordinary land conveyance, including rural mail delivery, $41,938,000; mail service by air, $21,738,000 and mail service by water $2,705,000. This is for the year we are in. These are not inconsequential figures. There is no breakdown, however, given with regard to the rate for small service by air per pound.
I like the expression the Postmaster General used today. He said, and I agree with him, that the Post Office Department is giving top-flight service. It is giving top-flight service, true enough, particularly on first class mail moved by air. My question is this. I should like to know what rate the Post Office Department is paying air line carriers per pound for the mail which moves by air compared to the rate per pound for the mail moved by land, water conveyance, or otherwise.
My question before the public accounts committee was based on the fact that quite a few years ago I was advised by a very senior official of the Post Office Department in Canada, who was provoked about it, and I was provoked about it at the time and still am if it is still true, that when the Canadian government first began to move mail by air-the main carrier at that time was

June 2, 1967
Supply-Post Office
Trans-Canada Air Lines and before the members from the province of Quebec start to say that this is not its name I would say I am talking of 20 years ago-the president of Trans-Canada Air Lines, who was very jealous of his reputation as a businessman, stated that he was not going to see Trans-Canada Air Lines operated at a loss so long as he was president. Through negotiations with the Canadian government the president of Trans-Canada Air Lines secured payments for moving postal matter by air, which payments had no relation to the value of this service. As a result of receiving large payments from the Post Office Department for moving mail by air, Trans-Canada Air Lines had very fine financial statements.
Now, the volume of mail moved by air has greatly increased over what it had been in the past. I should like to know whether there is some rate per pound or per hundredweight which has been established on mail going by air, as compared to the mail which may move by land, water, or other means of conveyance in this country. Are we paying too much for the conveyance of mail by air compared to what it could be moved for by other means? This is a question which in any privately owned business would be watched day by day. At the end of the month there would be a separate notation made concerning what the carrying charges were per pound by air, what they were by rail and what they were per pound by water, so the mail could be moved by the most economical means consistent with good service.
Are we still paying the air lines the rate they demand for moving mail by air without any regard to what the rate is per pound for the business handled?
Members of the Liberal party are sometimes colloquially called the government, but the cabinet makes certain it is called the government and asks that a private member should support the cabinet when it makes what they call government policy. As members of the party we are not asked what the rates should be for special service. We are just asked to O.K. the particular item in the votes. Since this matter is not raised either in the party caucus or in the policy conventions of the party, I should like to ask why we convey all across Canada for nothing these publications which come in from all foreign countries. This question has been raised over the past 25 years with whatever government was in power. I will say one thing; every government was equal to the task of doing nothing during that time.

The hon. member for Lambton-Kent, speaking a little earlier in this discussion, referred to the fact that I raised this matter last year. I am referring to it again this year, and I expect I will refer to it as long as I am a member of this house, because the answer is always given that nothing can be done about it for five years until the next world postal congress meets, at which time the international postal rates are discussed.
The international rates are set for five years. There has been a meeting of this international postal congress since I came into the house five years ago this month and nothing has been done about it, although I personally raised the point in private conversation not with the present Postmaster General but with other postmasters general, and was assured that the matter would be taken up at the meeting which was to be held first in Rio de Janeiro and then, because of some trouble down there, was held in Vienna, Austria.
The international postal rates were not changed in the slightest. As the hon. member for Lambton-Kent correctly quoted me saying a year ago, we now move any Danish publication which might enter Canada at Montreal right clean through to Nanaimo or Victoria, British Columbia for exactly the same remuneration as the Danish post office moves a Canadian newspaper from Copenhagen to some outer island in Denmark, and that is exactly zero; because there is no division of the revenue received from publications by post offices in the originating country.
I have also raised the point-with regard to the tens of thousands of mail subscriptions to United States publications which cross the international border into this country every day. If you do not wish to accept tens of thousands every day, then average it on a day by day basis for the weekly publications, the monthly publications and the quarterly publications which come into this country by international mail service under the international agreement whereby Canadian publications are given the same rights in other countries that the Canadian post office gives to foreign publications in this land; but consider the distances which we move those publications and consider the disparity in circulation between United States publications selling in Canada and Canadian publications selling in the United States of America.
I have previously made the suggestion to wh ch I referred earlier in these remarks- and of course no action was taken-that on
June 2, 1967

certain days of the year the Post Office Department of Canada should hold up the second class mail originating outside the country in order to estimate the volume of second class mail coming into the country on which we receive no revenue. The suggestion that it be held up for one day so a check can be made to see how far the original subscriptions are moving and what is the weight of the mail, is based on the action of the Post Office Department over the past 20 years of holding up all parcel post mail for two days a year when they check to see what is the volume of parcel post mail crossing the border both ways and how far it is being transported. Then cheques are issued for the difference in weights and the difference in mileage by the country that is enjoying the advantage of parcel post mail under this international service.
Similar arrangements could be made in respect of second class mail. This would go a long way toward eliminating this deficit of $30 million which the Postmaster General has mentioned has accrued to the Canadian post office in the year ending March 31, 1967. Now we have a promised deficit for next year of $740 million. As a loyal Liberal I must state that I ran for parliament in 1962 because I did not like the deficits Mr. Fleming was piling up; but as a loyal Liberal I must say that Fleming evidently cannot do anything that we Liberals cannot do bigger.
[DOT] (12:50 p.m.)
Next year we are going to give you a real ripper of a deficit of $740 million, and I wonder what the post office deficit will be as a contribution to that figure. I tell you, Mr. Chairman, that the taxpayers are becoming a little fed up with the way money is cast around in this country with apparently little regard for any means of either cutting down expenditures or bringing in revenue to offset the expenditures being made.
I do not think the $30 million deficit in the postal service is at all necessary. This is one department of the government where, if the cabinet would take firm action, the deficit could be eliminated and eliminated very quickly, even though they have this international agreement on which they always rely when you talk about international mail crossing the border.
Will you please tell us how the deficit could be removed?

I have mentioned the holding up of second class mail at the border and
Supply-Post Office
checking to see what weight is coming in and how far it is going, and then asking the originating country to pay a certain rate per pound for moving this international mail over great distances. I have another suggestion in respect of second class mail. I know of no reason this country should carry small weekly newspapers free of charge within a certain distance of the office of publication. Having been in printing or in the newspaper business all my life, I have never been able to comprehend why this is done unless it is as a favour to the local publisher so he will always speak well of the local member of parliament, realizing he is being given a subsidy which is of some value to him.
I know of weekly newspaper publishers who mail all their papers to their readers because it costs them nothing, although it does require a little effort on the part of the circulation department. On the other hand I know of other weekly newspaper publishers who, because of the time required to wrap the papers and address them to their subscribers, even though there is no postage involved, tell their subscribers to come down to the office and pick up the papers. In this way they do not go through the local post office.
Why should there be an exemption from postal rates whereby local weekly newspapers do not pay postage at all for delivery within a certain area of the office of publication? Such a privilege is not granted to businessmen in any other line of endeavour. If the man is a seed merchant in a town and receives an order to send certain seeds to a farmer some distance away from the town where the man has his seed shop, he has to pay postage. However, if that farmer wants to take the weekly newspaper the newspaper does not have to pay postage. Why is there this discrimination in favour of the weekly newspaper publisher as opposed to other classes of businessmen who have to pay postage in respect of the service rendered by the post office?
I do not think the imposition of a reasonable postage charge on weekly newspapers would cost the weekly publishers a great deal of money, because they would ask their subscribers in the small towns of publication to come to the office and pick up the paper each week. They would only have to mail papers to those subscribers on rural routes or those living some distance away who may have been sons or daughters of the community and still like to read the weekly paper. This would eliminate the practice on the part of weekly publishers which I believe is helping to create

June 2, 1967
Supply-Post Office
the deficit, and would do away with this largesse from the Canadian taxpayer. Please keep in mind that these publishers are not accepting largesse from the Canadian government but from the Canadian taxpayer, who has to foot the bill for this $30 million deficit in the Post Office Department for the year ending March 31, 1967.
There is another classification which I think should be changed by the government, and it could be done by setting another rate. Why should we give a special rate in respect of agricultural publications moving across the country? It is fine to say that agricultural publications are being read by the farmers and this helps the farmers increase productivity in Canada. The more the farmer learns from his weekly or monthly periodical the better off the country is, and it is argued that we should sustain weekly farm publications in order that knowledge and advice may be brought to the farmer in respect of his work.
Please bear in mind that farmers do not own these publications. The two largest farm publications in Canada today are owned by possibly the two wealthiest families in the country. I know of no reason for granting a special postage rate in respect of the Family Herald and Weekly Star out of Montreal, or the Free Press Prairie Farmer out of Winnipeg. One is owned by McConnell and the other is owned by Sifton. Heaven knows that the Canadian taxpayer should not be asked to subsidize families like those simply because they publish farm publications with circulations in rural communities. This is the type of subsidization which is not readily apparent to the Canadian taxpayer, but when he is hit with a $30 million deficit he would surely like to know how it came about. I believe the time has long since passed when the taxpayer should have been told exactly how these deficits accrue.
Do these publishers have political affiliations?

I understand from reading editorials in the Winnipeg Free Press regarding the armed forces unification bill that they were not too happy with the present government, but historically in the past they have had a connection with the Liberal party. I may say in answer to the member for Winnipeg South Centre that his question would have been more appropriate six months ago, before the time of the unification bill. I believe I understand the point he is endeavouring to make by his question.

In regard to the Montreal situation, I am sure it does not require a single member of parliament such as myself to provide the answer. It is self evident to every member of the house whether there are political affiliations involved there. I might point out that this largesse to the families owning these agricultural papers has always been continued no matter which party was in government, whether it was under R. B. Bennett, Mr. Diefenbaker, Mr. King, Mr. St. Laurent, or the present Prime Minister. Possibly political affiliations have had nothing to do with the situation, but this is a situation that should be corrected for the benefit of the Canadian taxpayer.
I should like to make another point in connection with rates of postage on second class mail, but it is now one o'clock and if it is agreeable to the committee I will call it one o'clock unless there is a desire that I should continue.
No, it is one o'clock.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: Order. House again in committee of supply, estimates of the department of the Postmaster General for the fiscal year ending March 31, 1968, vote No. 1.

Mr. Chairman, when the midday break came I stated that I wanted to make some comments with regard to the zone rate of postage on second and third class mail as another means of reducing last year's deficit of $30 million in the Post Office Department. The question of imposing in Canada a zone rate of postage on newspapers and magazines has been discussed times without number ever since the United States introduced a zone rate of postage more than 30 years ago.
The discussions I as a businessman have had with the Canadian government on numerous occasions as to why they did not have zone rate postage have always resulted in my being told in effect that the Canadian people would not like to see a zone rate of postage imposed because the subscription rates of national magazines would probably be raised to
June 2, 1967

meet the increased postage. I do not know what the difference is between paying a low subscription rate and then having to pay for a post office deficit, and paying a high rate for publications and not having a post office deficit. The zone rate of postage has been imposed in the United States for a long time and is a successful way of making the publishers pay a just and fair proportion of the cost of handling their publications in the mail.
The interesting thing about the zone rate of postage is that in the United States the rate does not vary on the editorial content. In this way there is no interference by the government, through the means of the post office, in the dissemination of editorial news or views to the nation. The rate goes up according to the zones through which the publication may travel and according to its advertising content. There is a low rate for the first or local zone and a higher rate for the second zone. If it moves through a third zone there is a higher rate and if it moves into a fourth zone there is again a higher rate, and so on.
It is interesting to remember that those great Canadian publications Time and Reader's Digest, which were given Canadian citizenship overnight although it takes a human being five years to obtain it, can be mailed in Montreal and travel the breadth of Canada from the west side of Vancouver Island to the east side of Newfoundland for the one rate of postage. They cost the taxpayers of Canada money every year because they do not pay their full mailing charges. Yet when these publications are mailed from the office of their publication in the United States they pay a zone rate of postage to move through the states.
Time and Reader's Digest are published simultaneously in a number of centres. This reduces the time consumed in transmission by mail in addition to reducing the cost of zone rate postage. When Time used to be published only in New York city and was mailed across the nation it travelled through a large number of zones. The same situation applied to Reader's Digest. Now that they are published simultaneously in a number of centres, their mailing may only take them through three zones. It is interesting to compare the situation that exists in Canada and the United States with regard to these publications. In the United States they have to pay a zone rate of postage according to the mileage travelled and the amount of advertising carried, whereas in Canada they go from the Atlantic to the Pacific with only one charge, no matter how many miles they travel.
Supply-Post Office
For the Canadian government to argue that they should not impose a zone rate of postage is ridiculous, because the Canadian government right now agrees with Canadian National Railways charging passenger fares according to the distance travelled. You cannot travel by railroad from Ottawa to Almonte for the same price as from Ottawa to Vancouver. But a publisher in Ottawa can mail his newspapers from Ottawa to Vancouver for the same price as from Ottawa to Almonte. On the railway you cannot send freight from Ottawa to Vancouver for the same rate as from Ottawa to Almonte. The freight rate is gauged according to the mileage travelled. You cannot send an express parcel from here to Carleton Place for the same rate as from here to Vancouver. You cannot send a telegram via Canadian National from here to Smiths Falls for the rate you would have to pay if you sent it to Vancouver. But if you are a magazine or newspaper publisher you can mail your publications for exactly the same rate no matter what the distance travelled. This is grossly unfair.
[DOT] (2:40 p.m.)
In so far as Air Canada fares for passengers are concerned, they are set according to the mileage covered. The hon. member for Timmins pointed out the other day how much those rates jump when you even cover an extra 12 miles in a flight from Timmins to Ottawa. If the government is authorizing, through these government owned agencies such as Canadian National Railways and Air Canada, rates for passengers, freight and express according to the mileage traversed, then surely the government can authorize postage rates according to the mileage traversed. It is a basic fact of business that the farther anything is carried and the greater the weight, then the carrying charges are set accordingly.
The C.B.C. is another crown corporation. They are always emphasizing this fact. They are only asking for $143 million this year from the Canadian taxpayers, so if that does not make them a crown agency I do not know what does. However, you cannot advertise over a C.B.C. station in Ottawa and expect to reach listeners in Vancouver or Halifax, Nova Scotia for the one charge on the one radio station. On the other hand, if you advertise in an Ottawa newspaper, that newspaper can be sent to readers in Vancouver or Halifax. You can reach them through the newspaper and as a result of the payment of one postal carrying charge. If you wanted to reach people across the nation by radio you would have to buy time on a large number of radio stations and

June 2, 1967
Supply-Post Office
obtain a network service. The cost would go up according to the area you were covering with your radio message.
These are three government agencies which impose charges according to mileage involved. This is not the case with postal services. We do not have zone rates tor postage. I am convinced that the second class postage deficit could be eliminated in part by not allowing cheaper rates for newspapers having less than 10,000 circulation. Lord Thomson happens to own the Kamloops Sentinel in British Columbia, with a circulation of 8,510. He also owns the Kelowna Courier with a circulation of 6,505 and the Nanaimo Free Press with a circulation of 8,415. On all of these publications he pays 33J per cent less than other newspapers such as the Woodstock Sentinel and the Sudbury Star which he also owns.
The committee on public accounts, under the chairmanship of the hon. member for Wellington South, presented report No. 21 dated Thursday, October 13, 1966. This report contains some very interesting comments with regard to the deficit on second class mail. The hon. member for Lambton-Kent made reference to it this morning and quoted from committee reports pointing out that the loss incurred by the Post Office Department could be entirely eliminated if there were reasonable rates for second class mail. I should like to read a paragraph from report No. 21. The chairman of the public accounts committee is in the house at the moment. I am reading from page 1007 of the report of the public accounts committee:
The committee feels that there is something wrong when no action has been taken with respect to, and apparently very little consideration given to, its recommendation on this matter.
The reference is to second class postage rates.
The committee first drew the matter to the attention of the house in its third report 1958 and, while minor changes have been made, the annual loss has continued to increase and the committee is of the opinion that sufficient consideration has not been given to the solution of this problem. It considers it essential that the Post Office Department or parliament immediately find ways and means of covering the loss of the Post Office Department in handling second class mail without this being done at the expense of other classes of mail, keeping in mind, however, the need of assistance to small independently owned newspapers circulating in rural areas.
This is the report of the public accounts committee. They point out that nobody pays any attention to their recommendations. Yet we have men standing up in this house extolling the great value of the committee system.

Well, I guess you can extol the great value of the system and pay no attention to the reports produced and see that they do not interfere with the operation of the government in any way. Here is the public accounts committee pointing out in black and white that nobody is paying any attention to them.
The report was passed unanimously, by the way.

I am glad to have that interjection indicating that the report was passed unanimously. I do not know whether the report will rate any higher with the cabinet than if it had been passed on division. However, I am glad to note that it was passed unanimously. I should like to see some action taken. All I am trying to do is to eliminate the second class postage deficit for the Post Office Department and thus reduce the national deficit of the government as a whole. We must remember that many mickles make a muckle. If we can eliminate the deficit of one department, perhaps we can eliminate the deficits of all and we will get a balanced budget.
I must say I do not care a great deal for the little tail on that paragraph in the report, "keeping in mind, however, the need of assistance to small independently owned newspapers circulating in rural areas''. There is another area of free postal service and it involves the little weeklies. The dailies of less than 10,000 circulation have a 33J per cent lower rate. As I have said, Lord Thomson owns the Kamloops Sentinel, the Kelowna Courier and the Nanaimo Free Press. Then there are the Prince George Citizen with a circulation of 10,435 and the Prince Rupert News with a circulation of 4,045. These two newspapers are owned by the same publisher. The Citizen has a higher rate of postage than the News. Does one newspaper publisher need to have support from the Canadian taxpayer because he prints the Prince Rupert News but no similar support when he prints the Prince George Citizen"!
If we skip across the country to Newfoundland we come up with the interesting fact that the St. John's Evening Telegram, with a circulation of 41,000, is owned by the Herder family which also owns the Corner Brook Western Star which has a circulation of 9,717. The taxpayer subsidizes the Western Star because its postage rate is one cent a pound, while for the St. John's Evening Telegram the postage rate is a cent and a half a pound. Does the owner of the St. John's
June 2, 1967

Evening Telegram and the Corner Brook Western Star need to be subsidized because one of his papers does not have a circulation of 10,000?
I have mentioned Lord Thomson more than once. The Southam chain is one of the great newspaper chains in Canada. They own the Medicine Hat News, which has a circulation of 7,452. This newspaper pays less postage per pound than the Calgary Herald which the Southams also own. In Saskatchewan there are four daily newspapers, two of which are owned by Thomson and two are owned by the Siftons. Outside of giving the Sifton interests assistance on agricultural newspapers which move more cheaply than do the Sifton dailies in Saskatchewan, we have the two Thomson newspapers, the Moose Jaw Times-Herald and the Prince Albert Herald, being subsidized through the Post Office Department, but there is no such subsidy for the Regina Leader Post or the Saskatoon Star-Phoenix. They are owned by the Siftons and have a circulation of more than 10,000.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: Order, I must advise the hon. member for York-Humber that the time allotted to him has expired.
Carry on.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: Does the hon. member wish to continue?
I should like to make a summation.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: Does the committee consent to the hon. member continuing his remarks?
Agreed.

I want to thank the committee for allowing me to continue. I should like to sum up what I have been saying before and after the mid-day break. I have been making suggestions to the Post Office Department but in no way am I criticizing the Postmaster General. The responsibility is that of the cabinet and the government, and I believe that action should have been taken long ago to eliminate the deficit on second class mail mentioned by the public accounts committee.
In order to save the time of the committee I should like to sum up by pointing out that I have been recommending for some years past that we should eliminate the losses incurred on second class mails coming into Canada across the international border from the originating country. I have explained that in detail in the past and I gave some details again 27053-70J
Supply-Post Office
this morning. While this may take time because of the fact that the World Postal Congress meets only once every five years, I would point out that Right Hon. Louis St. Laurent, when prime minister of Canada, imposed a tax on United States publications because he was so incensed over the loss that was accruing to the Canadian government. When he was advised he could not do it because of an international agreement, Mr. St. Laurent told the United States he could not care less where an international agreement was unfair to Canada. I believe that these international agreements with the United States postal service could be negotiated separately instead of having to wait for five years.
To get down to the domestic or local scene, we could make some improvements right away in postal rates that would help to eliminate the $30 million deficit. The government could eliminate the free postal service for weekly newspapers in Canada. In "Canadian Advertising Rates and Data" you will find on page 74 a list of the weeklies owned by Lord Thomson of Fleet, who is being subsidized on his Canadian weekly newspapers while he publishes the London Sunday Times and the London Morning Times in London, England.
[DOT] (2:50 p.m.)
I have suggested that we should raise the postage rate on agricultural publications to the same rate as that charged for the larger dailies. I have suggested a zone rate of postage for all magazines and newspapers so that they will pay according to the distance traversed. I have recommended that the favouritism shown to the small dailies should be eliminated. We should also eliminate the favouritism that is shown to some monthly publications compared with weekly publications, though I have not dealt with that matter today.
In conclusion, Mr. Chairman, I should like to emphasize that I think the Canadian cabinet and the Canadian government should immediately eliminate the free service that is given the weekly press by the Post Office Department. It should raise the rates of postage on agricultural papers. It should impose a zone rate of postage on all publications and bring the small dailies up to the same rate as that charged on the larger ones. I do not like a $30 million deficit in the Post Office Department. I am not criticizing the Postmaster General, but I am certainly directing my remarks to the cabinet as a whole.

June 2, 1967
Supply-Post Office

I have a few brief observations with regard to the Post Office Department, Mr. Chairman. First of all I should like to endorse the remarks of the previous speaker in connection with the concern felt about the drain on the profits of the Post Office Department. I may say I have always had a keen interest in the operations of this department, an interest which springs, I suppose, primarily from the fact that I had an uncle who was a postmaster in the city of Guelph.
I sincerely hope that the time is not far distant when this or some succeeding government will give consideration to putting the post office operations into the hands of a crown-owned corporation. I believe that the whole department needs revitalizing. We have been going along in the same old way and in the same old rut for so may years that it is time to revitalize the department and put it under the charge of a crowm corporation.
I think of the rural mail routes which were laid out in the horse and buggy days and are still in existence. Granted, they have been revised to a certain extent, but there are many things which can be done to introduce a much better perspective with regard to rural postal delivery than is the case today. I think also of certain rural post offices, small, untidy, disgraceful places in which to handle the Queen's mail. was brought in at a time when so many of the carriers were people who operated farms, when the extra horse required did not take too much feed and the upkeep of the buggy was not too great. These farmers got into the habit of tendering for mail contracts at such a low figure that they were entirely unprofitable.
We who drive automobiles today are told many times by the insurance companies that under normal circumstances we cannot operate an automobile for less than ten cents a mile. I should like to say here that I appreciate the co-operation I have received from the transportation section of the Post Office Department, which has always been of the best. I sincerely hope that the Postmaster General will consider all representations made here on behalf of the rural mail carriers and revise this legislation, so that it can be brought up to date and in keeping with the times.
