In my area, and in much of Saskatchewan, great efforts have been made during the last few years to organize what are known as regional libraries, with central depots about 150 miles from the rim of each district. This means books have to be transported that far. It is not likely they would be sent by post, but in the outlying areas there are subdivisions which also require delivery of library books.
Since attempts are being made to improve the education of our citizens it would be most

June 2, 1967
Supply-Post Office
unfair and unwise to put any handicap in the way of those attempts. To raise the library book postal rate in effect would do that. Although we all want to see second class mail in particular bear its full cost, this is one area in which relief would be in the national interest. I hope the minister will consider the matter.
I also think the increase in the cost of registration of mail is rather excessive. I suppose cost studies have been made and that the minister feels the costs warrant the increase. If this is true then I have no objection, but I would like to know that such studies have been made.

speakerposition: N.D.P. House Leader; Whip of the N.D.P.
speechtext: Mr. Chairman, like most hon. members who have spoken today, including in particular my hon. friend from Winnipeg South Centre, I should like to commend the Postmaster General-
I did not commend him.

speakerposition: N.D.P. House Leader; Whip of the N.D.P.
speechtext:
Oh, in your heart you did. I should like to commend the Postmaster General on the quiet efficiency with which he presides over this important department. I wish him well, and I trust he will continue to exercise that quiet efficiency during the interesting days ahead when collective bargaining comes into play. This is going to be an important era in the public service of Canada, and I am sure we all realize that the postal department is one where this desirable method of arranging for conditions of work and wages will be put to the test. I am sure the minister is as anxious as I am to see it work, and I wish him well, as he presides over this department at this important time. I should also like to say that as a member from the city of Winnipeg I appreciate the courteous service and attention that is given by the postmaster of that city and his employees to those of us who have occasion to send a considerable volume of mail into our constituencies.
If I might be pardoned one other preliminary word, I have noticed with interest that a good many members have associated themselves with the Post Office Department in various ways. The Postmaster General has an interesting connection of his own. My claim to fame in this connection is that my grandmother was postmistress for many years at an important point in Shelburne county, Nova Scotia, and for many years after her death the post office there continued to be known as Knowles' post office. Unfortunately the previous government found out about it, and during that regime Knowles' post office was discontinued, I do not quite know why. But

perhaps something might now be done about it.
However, Mr. Chairman, I rose because of just one issue which I would like to bring to the attention of the minister. I did so by letter and he answered me very courteously, but I still feel the issue should be looked into. I speak on behalf of quite a number of casual employees who get a good deal of work in the Winnipeg post office, and appreciate it. However, they find that despite the fact that they have worked as casuals for many years they never accumulate enough continuous employment to merit their being granted holiday pay. I wrote the minister about this, indicating that I was aware of the regulations. He appreciated that fact but reminded me of them, and said the difficulty is that if people do not get 30 days work on a continuous basis they cannot qualify for the percentage that is allowed under regulations for holiday pay.
The people affected find it a strange coincidence that the amount of work which necessitates their beings called in can be very heavy, but all of a sudden just at the point when they might have enough days to qualify for holiday pay they are laid off and taken back again later. They never get this holiday pay which is provided under regulations affecting government employees, on a basis similar to that provided to those who are under federal labour jurisdiction by virtue of the Canada Labour (Standards) Code.
I would ask that this matter be examined again. I realize the regulations in this respect are not regulations of the Post Office Department. They are regulations that apply to government employees generally. Maybe the minister could do something about these regulations, but at least I think he should make sure that the suspicions of the people affected are not valid. The suspicions could be removed if on occasion these people with many years of casual service could qualify for holiday pay and I urge the minister to see that this is done.

Mr. Chairman, the hon. member for Queens voiced valid concern over the lack of provision for a commemoration stamp in memory of our first prime minister, Sir John A. Macdonald. I myself expressed this concern in questions during the first session of this parliament, and on this occasion I want to support the hon. member and deplore this lack.
I have a question relating to special delivery to rural post offices. It seems to me there
June 2, 1967

is no point in mailing a special delivery letter to very small rural post offices because they do not have any special facilities to deliver them. Mail at these points is picked up only once or twice a week, and if a special delivery letter happens to arrive after a person has picked up his mail, how is he to be made aware of the fact? I believe some compensation ought to be given to the local postmaster for delivering such a letter, or for informing the recipient by telephone of its presence. In many small rural communities although phones may be only a few miles apart calls between them are long distance calls. Is there any compensation paid to local postmasters for delivery of special delivery letters?

Mr. Chairman, I would like to bring three short specific points to the minister's attention in the hope that they will receive serious consideration. One deals with the town of Ridgetown, Ontario, and the post office facilities in it. A new post office building has been postponed for a long time, and for many reasons. I would request that the minister lend his weight to seeing that the new building is constructed at an early date. Indeed, Mr. Chairman, it was so bad that complaints came in about the despicable state of repair of the building, which formerly had been used as a municipal building, fire hall, and post office. The fact is that complaints did come to the government department, together with a request that the broken windows be repaired, that the lawns be mown and that the facilities be taken care of because the property was such an eyesore.
[DOT] (4:50 p.m.)
The second matter has to do with the hardships suffered by those in small local post offices. I do not feel that in this regard there should be such strict adherence to the regulations as there has been. I am not one who believes that regulations should be circumvented in any way, but certainly the requirement which requires people to return to their post offices for one hour on Saturday afternoon works a hardship on the people who run these post offices in some of the local areas. Normally they would be free at noon on Saturday and would have the afternoon off. Under the proposed regulations, in order to fit in with the labour standards, they are required to return to open the post office for one hour only.
On the same day they may have been forced to close the post office at eleven o'clock and could not issue mail during the lunch hour. I believe that in circumstances such as
Supply-Post Office
this strict adherence to the regulations should not circumvent good sense in this regard. I have no quarrel at all with the people in the local administration because they have done everything they could. They too however are bound by the regulations. I am wondering therefore whether in situations such as this the minister could make some provision so that the whole pattern of a community is not interrupted, so that the people who pick up their kiddies from school could, as they have done through the years, pick up their mail at the same time during the lunch hour, and so that when the women are shopping they could pick up their mail on their way home at noon. In this way the whole routine of the community would not be upset due to the 40 hour week.
There is one other matter with which I should like to deal. This also has to do with strict adherence to the regulations. Surely when one lives within 50 feet or 100 yards of the area where the rural district stops and the urban district begins there must be a way to circumvent the regulations so that a person who is aged or incapacitated is not inconvenienced or subjected to dire hardship. Due to the fact that some people live just beyond the pale they are put to the inconvenience of having to resort to the goodness of their neighbours in having their mail looked after. I am sure the minister and those in the department will take care of these things. I am sure also that these regulations were never intended to work a hardship on the people concerned, but rather were intended as guide lines to help provide an efficient service. I would really hope that the minister would give consideration to the problems I have outlined.

Mr. Chairman, I know the members of the house are very anxious to get these estimates through before five o'clock. I should like to make a few comments on the general points which were brought up during this discussion, First, I should like to thank all hon. members who took part in this debate for the constructive way they have presented their criticisms and for the comments they made in respect of myself personally. I appreciate this and I shall take the advice of the hon. member for Winnipeg South Centre, that I do not permit myself to be carried away by these comments.
As most hon. members are aware, on the one hand I was asked to try to balance the budget and get rid of the deficit, and on the other hand I received criticism in respect of

June 2, 1967
Supply-Post Office
the recent increased costs. If I increased only the third class services, this was because I could do it on my own without asking for the approval of parliament. So far as the second class services are concerned, I intend in the fall to ask for authority in this regard from parliament.
With regard to c.o.d.'s, special deliveries, library books, and so on, we know exactly how much these services cost. Even if there is a slight increase in some instances and a considerable increase in others, we are still losing money on these items we are delivering.
Much has been said about the rural routes. This is a situation which I intend to change as a result of the amendments to the Post Office Act which I plan to bring in during the fall. There will be some changes. Let us say that perhaps these rural couriers for many years have been the worst political victims in this department. It was, though perhaps not a rule, at least a well established practice that if one of these contracts had ended, the government which was in power would ask the member of parliament for that constituency or the defeated candidate whether in his opinion the contract should be renewed -because the Postmaster General has the right to renew these contracts-or whether tenders should be asked on it.
I stopped this practice, Mr. Chairman, because I believe this is something which has been very bad for the poor rural couriers, who are endeavouring to make a living. I do not believe it should always be necessary for them to retender every four years, because in order to be reasonably sure they would obtain the contract they sometimes would tender at an amount lower than that which they had been receiving under the previous contract. This would mean that they would have to wait two more years in order to have it readjusted. I believe if the regional manager finds that a rural courier is doing a good job, that rural courier should have his contract renewed automatically.
Readjustments are being made every second year. One exception, however, is that in respect of the last increases which were given we added an amount for the contribution to the Canada Pension Plan, and another amount in lieu of the holidays, which cannot be given.
So far as stamps are concerned, although we have had many criticisms of our stamps, people who know about philately say that our stamps are of very good quality. I was asked

exactly what the procedure is in this regard. We decide how many stamps should be issued in a year and what things should be commemorated. We ask some well known artist to design stamps for us. Sometimes we receive ten, 12 or 15 different drawings. It is up to the Postmaster General to decide which of these should be accepted. I must say that on some occasions when there are seven, eight or ten different designs I do not have too much choice. It becomes a matter of choosing the one which is not the worst. This makes it more difficult. If we were to form a committee to select the stamps, I believe this would be merely an effort to place the responsibility on someone else when, I believe, the Postmaster General should accept that responsibility.
[DOT] (5:00 p.m.)
The opening remarks in respect of this discussion were made by the hon. member for Lambton-Kent. He seemed to be very confused concerning the manner in which the estimates are prepared. I must say that the post office is one of seven or eight departments which have developed a system of program budgeting as recommended by the Glassco Commission. One thing still not shown in the estimates is the amount the department has to pay the Department of Public Works for buildings. This will be shown, and I am sorry the report of the Postmaster General was not printed by the Queen's Printer in time for distribution before consideration of my estimates. I understand they will be completed in a few days.
In the past I have followed the practice of answering by letter hon. members' questions raised during the consideration of my estimates, and I intend to do the same thing this time.
Perhaps I could cover one other point raised by the hon. member for Wellington South concerning the proposal to make this department a crown corporation. A study is presently being carried out to determine whether this would be a good idea for Canada and for the employees. I know that in other countries where postal services are performed by a crown corporation they do not have services as good as ours. I also know in other countries which have not changed to a crown corporation their service is much worse than ours. We must determine by study whether this would improve the service in Canada, and if those studies indicate that there would be an improvement I will be the first one to*
June 2, 1967



press the government for the establishment of a crown corporation.
Such a move would reduce the size of the cabinet.

That might be true, but perhaps we would then be looking for a president for the crown corporation. Maybe you would be interested.
I do not believe there is much point in commenting on this suggestion without having all the figures and facts resulting from the study. My deputy minister was in London in May to meet his counterpart there to find out how the crown corporation is operating, and this is part of the study which is taking place.
One or two questions were raised by the hon. member for York-Humber regarding the rates and costs of our air service through Air Canada. At one time the rate was as high as $9.25 per ton mile. We are now paying 52.1 cents per ton mile.
Mr. Chairman, may I continue?

speakerposition: N.D.P. House Leader; Whip of the N.D.P.
speechtext: Don't ask; just carry on.

Agreed.
Let us not see the clock.

Agreed.
Just for five minutes.

The hon. member for Lambton-Kent asked about publicity by the use of film, and said that he had not seen any as yet. We are using clips on television at Christmas time urging people to mail early. We also have a centennial film to be used as a publicity vehicle to show the history and growth of the Canadian post office in conjunction with the history and growth of Canada.
The hon. member for Vancouver East made quite a plea in respect of the Pony Express employees in Vancouver. It is not easy for a government which decides, for good reasons, to take over a certain service; but I think a government department should be allowed to do so when it is felt advantageous to the department. There is a problem in relation to the employees who worked for this contractor, but the contractor was not sure of having the contract permanently. I believe that we should ask for tenders every four years, so
Supply-Post Office
that these contracts are made subject to tender.
Perhaps I should say that in big cities we cannot always call for tenders because there is no one else but the present contractor who has the number of trucks and employees necessary to operate this type of service. In some of these cities the contracts have been renewed as a result of not calling for tenders for 12 to 15 years. I do not think this is the good or the right way to run a business. We should make it possible to have competition in this area of the postal service.
Having regard to the Pony Express service, we received 291 applications from people other than the employees of the Pony Express for the jobs available, and they were agreeable to accepting the rate which everyone else doing this work in the Post Office Department is receiving. Incidentally this rate was agreed to by the postal unions. Of the 291 applications, there were 11 from post office employees, four of which qualified. We received three applications from employees of the Pony Express. One was qualified; one did not pass the driver's test and one was not suitable for the job. We are trying our best to help these people, but we still have problems because many of them cannot qualify under the regulations of the Post Office Department. We hope that as a result of the experience we are gaining our transportation services will prove satisfactory.
The hon. member for Springfield raised a question about rates of pay for postmasters in rural areas throughout the country. Let me say that this year the increases granted varied between 7 per cent and 29 per cent and they were interim increases. As a result these postmasters received the biggest increase they have ever had. We are also using these increased figures in a general reclassification of postmasters and assistants in order to create a better balance in respect of the pay they receive in relation to the work they are performing.
The hon. member also referred to third class mail lying on counters. I will look into this situation, but I must say this is the first time I have heard about it.
Mr. Chairman, I think that covers about everything, although perhaps I should say something about the problems raised by the hon. member for Gaspe. I think we have made great improvement in postal services in that area over the past few years. People are beginning to realize that we are giving much better service. At a later time I will provide

June 2, 1967
Canada Elections Act
that hon. members with the explanations for which he has asked.
I shall also look into problems relating to casual employees. We have had some difficulty in this regard throughout the country, but we are faced with certain difficulties because of the regulations of the Public Service Act, and we have to be guided by this act.
[DOT] (5:10 p.m.)

The hon. member for Trois-Rivieres (Mr. Mongrain) spoke to me of the philatelic gallery which is there and which I had the pleasure to visit. I can say that Mr. Levesque who built and owns this gallery has done extraordinary work to try to retrace the history throughout the eras and we are most interested in getting, in the department, a kind of curator who could organize a philatelic gallery so that people who come to visit the capital could see the riches we now have in the department. The department owns an extraordinary number of stamps which are not exhibited, but held in files and it would be most interesting for the Canadian people to have the opportunity of seeing these items.

That is about all I have to say, Mr. Chairman. As I said before, any answers that I could not give today will be given by me in the next few weeks.
Item agreed to.

subtopic: PROHIBITION OF PUBLICATION OF STRAW POLL RESULTS DURING CAMPAIGN
PROHIBITION OF PUBLICATION OF STRAW POLL RESULTS DURING CAMPAIGN
speechtext:
the second reading of Bill No. C-3, to amend the Canada Elections Act (publication of straw poll results).
tMr. Cdte (Longueuil).]
He said: Mr. Speaker, there are a number of different types of public bills on the order paper and I think this one fits into a very broad category in which there should be discussion by all persons concerned, rather than a member trying to express an independent point of view, as happens with respect to many of the bills dealt with in this hour. The purpose of this bill is not to eliminate the taking of public opinion polls. I think the opinion polls that have been taken have had a fairly uncanny accuracy. It is surprising when one looks back at the results projected in elections, in particular, and sees the accuracy these polls have displayed. I think this raises a doubt, however, as to whether this particular tool should be allowed to be used during an election.
It is interesting to note that in conducting a straw poll or an opinion poll you are taking the opinion of a very small section of the population. If it is done scientifically and covers a broad spectrum of public opinion, though the number may be very small the result will probably produce the fairly accurate opinion of those asked the specific question. This of course raises, in a political sense, a great deal of difficulty. It was interesting to watch last year the manipulations that took place in political parties in the province of Ontario. My political party has been no less involved than others in the taking of polls for the assessment of public opinion in respect of its philosophy. It was interesting last year to read that the Liberals in conducting their opinion poll found the Conservatives to be in a very low position in the eyes of those polled. They found they were not too well off and surprisingly agreed that the New Democrats in Ontario had made very large gains. The Conservatives took a poll which showed they were not quite so badly off, and they also indicated that the N.D.P. had made very sizeable gains.
I have the opportunity of sitting on the executive of the Ontario section of my party, and sat in on a number of discussions where the enthusiasm which you might expect for these polls was totally absent. In fact a great deal of controversy was raised about what the results of these polls really meant, so much so that the executive finally decided to take an opinion poll of their own. They were going to do it very honestly. There was a difference of opinion in how we should word the question contained in the poll in order to achieve a result that we thought would be accurate. We did not want to achieve the result we would like to see, but one which was accurate. There
June 2, 1967

was considerable difficulty in a number of people deciding what question should be asked in order to obtain an accurate sampling of the electorate, rather than asking the kind of question that would get a huge majority of "yesses" in answering the question asked.
I think anyone who has been concerned with the taking of opinion polls will agree that they are only of value if the person asking the question has no interest in the result of the poll, other than in a scientific sense. The question has to be asked in such a way that it is not a leading question, such as: Have you quit beating your wife yet? It does not really make much difference whether the answer to that question is yes or no; the opinion poll indicates that you had been beating her in the past. This is a very easy type of question to set up. It seems to me that if you conduct an opinion poll during an election, you might as well not have the election. Certainly all the dictatorships and all the countries in which they have state newspapers conduct opinion polls wherein the question is oriented so that it will receive the required answer. This does not establish an opinion of the electorate; it is asking for the opinion of the electorate but deciding what the answer shall be.
If you check history you will see this is partly the reason why the national socialist or nazi party of Germany was able to win an overwhelming vote in 1936 or 1937. The question that is asked elicits only one answer, and anybody who is willing to cast a ballot provides that answer.
I believe that elections are an important and integral part of our democratic process. This is not to say that politicians and political parties have not a major role to play because I believe they do. I believe that election issues should be decided by a thinking, informed electorate on the facts which are provided. It seems to me that the electorate should have as much information provided as is possible, that political propaganda or even the popularity of an individual should play an important role. The news media should provide information on both the pro's and con's of all problems or issues. All the information possible should be provided to the electorate so they can make a decision.
[DOT] (5:20 p.m.)
Now, each of the political parties should have, and usually does have, the right to put forward its views in clear, informative way so 27053-71
Canada Elections Act
that the electorate is really an informed electorate and will make a decision in the national interest. It seems that if an opinion poll is conducted during an election campaign and the results are printed, there is a tendency for the public to be influenced by those results. There are of course many people who will say they want to be on the winning side. If there are many who take this attitude, then they are not going to make an intelligent decision.
I believe that opinion polls should be conducted. The only thing this amendment attempts to do is to prohibit the publication of the results of an opinion poll between the time an election is called and the time the election is held. The results can be made known of course afterwards, when they would not influence the election results.
Some members will say this is a restriction on the right of agencies to conduct opinion polls. However, this step has been taken in British Columbia. I have not been able to ascertain whether British Columbia experienced some unfortunate incident which caused the passage of legislation of this type. However, it has not been possible, under penalty of law, to conduct an opinion poll in British Columbia and publish the result during an election.
I believe there is some merit in the restriction I suggest. I believe it will become more and more important as political parties gain some equality in ability to get their message across to the people. As I say, changes may take place where political parties will be allowed a certain amount of money per voter to get their message across to the electorate.
I think most people will agree that political parties should be able to provide information about their platform and their record, and they should have an obligation to make the electorate understand the issues of the day and their role in these issues. This would enable the electorate to make a decision. I feel therefore if we are looking at amendments to the election act, that the publication of the results of opinion polls should be prohibited at certain times. The history of opinion polls in Canada has been unlike that of the United States. Our opinion polls have been fairly accurate in their forecasts. Sometimes you wonder whether the accuracy stems from the publication of these polls or whether this is an indication of the influence they have upon people.
I think everyone will agree that unless the questioner is totally unbiased or the question is asked in a way to elicit information, it

June 2, 1967
Canada Elections Act
would be very difficult indeed to make accurate forcasts on the basis of the poll being conducted. For this reason, I believe the question merits some study by a committee.
This matter should not be considered in a political way, but as to whether or not this prohibition will result in a more informed electorate, and electorate that is better able to make its own judgment. This may strengthen the role of democracy. I suggest that those who believe it will do so should support this bill, whereas those who believe these polls are a tool of politics should oppose the bill.
As I have said, I believe that each political party in Ontario has gone into this field. Evidently there is not going to be an election in Ontario this spring and that may be partly because of the publication of these opinion polls. This may have had some influence on the deicison not to hold an election, and that may be good or bad. I think it is unfair that the results of any poll should be published a few days before an election, if it has any influence on the electorate. I think most of us agree the attitude is wrong, but some person will say: I have to be on the winning side, and this looks like the winning side.
I say this, Mr. Speaker, knowing full well that from time to time the winning side may change. When I first thought of this idea, I probably thought of it because we may have been on the wrong side. Time may have changed that situation and opinion polls, properly conducted may be advantageous to us. However, I feel they should not be looked at in a narrow way if we are changing the elections act. We should make changes in a manner which will give us the best possible elections act, so as to develop an informed electorate and so that national interests can be served.

speechtext:
polls to evaluate their personal popularity.
The polls have grown so technical, so perfected, so accurate, that they enable the candidates to adjust their image, their aim to the wishes of their electors.
Even some very flexible American candidates can suddenly become more conservative or liberal or socialist according to the findings, the tastes of their electors, as revealed by those polls which have become very accurate.
It seems that the president of the United States is somewhat allergic to polls and his blood pressure goes up or down according to his popularity ratings.
There is no doubt that his policy, and probably several of his daily decisions are at least in part affected to some extent by those political polls.
Even the way the Viet Nam war is carried out cannot escape completely that natural reaction. In exaggerating a little, one might conclude that the fate of humanity can be decided on the results of a Gallup or a Lou Harris poll.
Here, in Canada, as the race for the leadership of a party, that is the leadership of the Conservative party, is gathering impetus, if ever it does, public opinion polls will enlighten us a little on the subject.
And I hope that these polls on the popularity of each candidate will bring to light the degree of popularity or lack of it of the respective candidates.
I think that the publication of such results, such soundings concerning the respective popularity of the candidates, would have a beneficial effect on the delegates to this convention and in fact on all Canadians who really want to understand the situation.
Actually, Mr. Speaker, public opinion is playing an increasingly important role in our society. I believe that a profound knowledge of the opinion of those who are governed can help those who govern.
In this respect, perhaps I may be allowed to quote a passage from this little book entitled "L'opinion publique", written by Alfred Sauvy and published by the French university press.
I quote from page 122:
The governed must express themselves-
It is necessary that the opinion of the public be known, that is the opinion of the whole body of the governed. The public authorities have not received from the electorate sufficient indications
27053-71 i
Canada Elections Act
on which to base their decisions on the issues coming up. No doubt, they lack a peremptory mandate, no doubt it could also be said that they must vote according to their conscience, taking into account a state of mind of those who have appointed them.
In no country, however, do the governed give up all participation between elections.
If a government and a parliament were to act in ignorance of the views of the governed, they would risk doing things which would not be approved and passing legislation or decrees that could not be enforced. Implementation requires a minimum of consent by the governed.
This is particularly true of internal policy. Foreign policy does not require as much checking with public opinion (and often goes without) as long as no contribution (tax, military, etc.) and too noticeable risks are involved.
Nevertheless, again in this area, the value of knowing the opinion of the governed is well understood.
Obviously, science as regards public opinion polls and technology is far from having achieved perfection and opinion polls err from time to time. It is nevertheless a science in process of development, but which would not achieve full growth should the state take upon itself to restrict it. Now I believe the bill introduced today, bill No C-3, is indeed a restriction of some kind in the final analysis.
At the time of the last general election in 1965, the Gallup poll had predicted a margin of 15 per cent in favour of the government's candidates, in favour of the Liberal party. As a matter of fact that margin, as we know, was reduced to 7 per cent over the Conservative party on election night. Peter Regenstreiff, of happy or unhappy memory, was another one, as we can remember, who was very much on the wrong track.
Needless to say that the newspapers in favour of the opposition parties made ample protests at the time. Allow me to quote, in this connection, a few excerpts from an editorial of the Fredericton Daily Gleaner, dated November 13, 1965. The article is under the heading: "Confusing the Electorate".

First of all, Mr. Speaker, I wish to quote the first two paragraphs of this editorial, which appeared in the Fredericton Daily Gleaner issue of Saturday, November 13, 1965:

We publish on another page today the Gallup poll's explanation of its failure to rightly assess the results of the federal election. It is, in our opinion, a most unsatisfactory explanation.

I now quote the last paragraph of that report entitled "Confusing the Electorate".

British Columbia's Attorney-General Robert Bonner says that political polls cast an unnatural light on electioneering and should be scrapped. We do not agree with him because we believe that freedom of expression demands that there shall be no barriers placed upon public opinion



Therefore, if the publication of Gallup type opinion polls taken to sound out the electorate was prohibited during political campaigns, as proposed in Bill No. C-3, the public would automatically be deprived of very valuable sources of information, even though they are not completely accurate yet, and even though that science requires more research. And, should the bill in question be passed, those sources of information, those opinion polls would still be available to the rich, the powerful, the potentates who would have the necessary funds for their own unpublished private polls.
I find it bit strange for a supporter of the socialist philosophy to advocate, in this house, a limitation of information media, a limitation in favour of the privileged classes, to the detriment of the worker and the man on the street who could not afford those polls which would still be avilable to those who are in a better financial position.
Mr. Speaker, I should also like to refer, in this connection, to a few paragraphs taken from an article published in the Ottawa Citizen on April 25, 1966 under the heading:

"Britons consider ban on election pollsters". I shall quote from that part of the article headed "Proof needed":
But since opinion polling is such a strong force, there would be dangers in allowing a government to prohibit it without considerable evidence that it is a serious evil, The Times adds.
An alternative would be to ban betting but The Times concludes that even this would not be
IMr. Dube.]
easy since betting undoubtedly would continue underground.
The pulse takers, who have turned opinion polls into big business, are watching the debate with some apprehension. Henry Durant, director of the British Gallup poll, suggests that without opinion polls, democracy would be operating in the dark.
"Can any argument be brought against polls which cannot also be brought against newspapers, radio and television?" he asks. "Is it better to have polls driven underground, undertaken by the rich for their private benefit rather than to have them made and published in the open?"

In closing, Mr. Speaker, I should like to echo the remarks of a journalist, an economist from London, as reported in the article already mentioned in the Ottawa Citizen.

I am quoting again from the article in the Ottawa Citizen of Monday, April 25, 1966:
To settle the whole argument, a member of The Economist magazine staff suggests with tongue in cheek; "Surely now is the time to conduct an opinion poll on the effect of opinion polls on voting behavior."

Mr. Speaker, I find myself in opposition to this measure. I think it is a potential curtailment of freedom of expression and it is certainly a curtailment of freedom of research. Many who are interested in public opinion sampling and in the taking of polls are not politicians. The behavioural scientists, sociologists, or political scientists are more than ever before engaged in this activity.
If this measure ever became part of the Canada Elections Act it would be a great denial, I think, to students in these fields. I quite agree that it is important to improve and make more scientific the conduct of public opinion polling. Hon. members are becoming amateur public opinion pollsters through the use of questionnaires. I find the amendment extremely restrictive. It would forbid the individual even by word of mouth to pass on information of certain kinds. For instance, you could not have information about what the taxi drivers are saying. Some persons go to meetings and ask: "What about the taxi drivers? What are they saying?" The answer is, "Oh, they are for" so and so. Such persons would even be prohibited from asking those questions and reporting the answers by this extremely restrictive act.
I am appalled by the suggestion that public opinion polls are fine until the election campaign starts. You have public opinion polls all the way through, and perhaps they indicate that a certain party has the allegiance of 65
June 2, 1967

per cent of the electorate. Then the election conies along; the people now know who the candidates are and what their views are. They know what the question is that they have to vote on. To say: "You cannot take polls, now that an election is on and publish the results" would mean that lingering through the election campaign would be the memory of a poll which was manifestly out of date, which was taken before the platforms were announced or before the issues were joined. In other words the only poll would be one that had been taken before the actual and real question could possibly have been posed to the electorate. This, I think, is the most regrettable part of this measure.
I presume the hon. member feels that the release of information taken from polls constitutes an improper influence on the voter. I am not so worried about that aspect, and I belong to the party that has been more often badly served than any other by public opinion polls of this country. In my opinion the release of results taken from the public opinion poll is only one factor which might influence the electorate, and during election campaigns many devices are designed to that end.
You have public meetings; you go in and say "Everybody is for me," and you hope that every newspaper will write, "The hall was packed." You even pay for an advertisement in the paper which says: The swing is to Joe, or to Bill, the people's candidate. In this way you are seeking to influence public opinion. If we are to forbid the professors of sociology from conducting polls, what about editorialists who in their editorials say: I think that such and such party will sweep the country? What about the pundits, the columnists, of which Charles Lynch is an example? Every time I read Charles Lynch saying that somebody will be defeated I mark that person down as somebody to be elected. In an election I should miss Charles Lynch. By reading him I know to whom to send my congratulatory letters in advance.
I am not worried about the spectre that the hon. member raises. It seems to me that by passing such legislation we should reveal a lack of faith in the rational processes of the people we represent. I think we can trust the people. They are not, surely, primarily motivated by the hope that they are to be on the winning side. If that were the case, some of us would never have gotten here, because there are many people in this chamber who were not billed as winners, and many times had elections followed public opinion polls
Canada Elections Act
there would have been an altogether different result. I think of 1957 as a prime example of this.
[DOT] (5:50 p.m.)
I am not impressed by British Columbia being cited as an example of a province where polls are banned. I see no real evidence that the political judgment of people in British Columbia is so much superior to that of Nova Scotia where we do have public opinion polls, and also I think extremely good judgment is known on "the day." I am always fearful of any legislation which seeks to protect the people against themselves. Let us have all the data which is available. Let us have the pollsters. If the average citizen knows that the Liberal party or the Conservative party has published a poll it would occur to him, I have no doubt, that there might be a certain element of bias attached to it.
The public knows that while polls are often right, they are frequently wrong, and I doubt that many people, when the crunch is on and they move into the silence of the poll booth, say to themselves: The public opinion polls tell us that so and so will win, and we want to make sure we prove the public opinion pollsters to be right. I believe they have more than that on their minds.
Let us trust the people. Give them the data. Let them put it through the mill of their own thinking, and I believe they will come up with a solution which is satisfactory to them and which is the result of free, democratic choice.

Today we have an electorate composed of people who are quite capable of making up their own minds. I do not think they will be bullied into voting one way or another just because newspapers publish public opinion polls.
What if we were to pass this legislation? Suppose we did make it illegal to use public opinion polls in the course of an election. What is there to prevent the United States television stations and radio stations across the border broadcasting all the public opinion polls taken in Canada, or even conducting such polls themselves and transmitting the

results as news to Canadians across the border?
We are told, after all, that 80 per cent of the Canadian population lives in a zone 100 miles north of the United States border. For this reason alone I would say it was nonsense for this house to be considering such a bill as is now before us, taking account of the news media which are now available. Even if we were to pass this bill it would not be effective; the news media would not be stymied.
I should like to cite the example of Mr. Regenstrief's prediction of the Social Credit upsurge in northern Quebec and other areas of Quebec in 1962. He was quite accurate in his prediction. But he did not create this movement. The ideas were there to begin with; he simply identified them. This I believe is what public opinion polls try to do.
We are told they have such a law as this in British Columbia. But what evidence is there to show it has been a good thing?

speechtext:
British Columbia does not have a Hansard either.
Is that a good thing? We have a more educated electorate today and, as I say, people will not be bullied into voting one way or another just because something appears in a newspaper.
I remember that in my own campaign in 1965 a person came from the headquarters of the opposition and stated, on the basis of a survey, that his party was well out in the lead in my riding. I believe this man's name was Goodman. Mr. Goodman was a little out on
that occasion. It just goes to prove that regardless of how often these statistics are published, people make up their own minds, basically, in accordance with their personal judgments. I do not think the publication of an opinion poll has any more influence on the public than many biased articles which appear in newspapers from time to time. I believe Canadians read their newspapers with a grain of salt, and that they make up their minds only after reading several newspapers or after listening to commentaries by various people. On this basis they decide what is closest to the truth.
In conclusion, let me say this. There is one thing of which every politician must be well aware. It is that we are all here with the consent of the public back home, and there are always people across Canada who can take our places. If anything were to happen to us today, the world would go on just the same. The electors would still carry on and make up their minds on the basis of what they think best for our country.
If I had time I would bring up the topic of the 1948 election in the United States. However, I see I do not have time in which to do so. I wish only to say I am quite satisfied to leave the fate of these polls to the good judgment of the Canadian people. I do not think we need attempt to stymie the news media in any way, because the good judgment of the electorate will make up the difference.
